text: State, transition, base cases, order: tables filled from small to large.

Recurrence (递推) builds the answer for size i from answers already found for smaller sizes, filling a table from the bottom up. Four things define it, and you should write all four down before coding: 1. State: what f[i] means, in one sentence. 2. Transition: how f[i] is made from earlier entries. 3. Base cases: the first entries, set by hand. 4. Order: fill so every entry needed is already known.

title: Climbing stairs: one or two steps at a time

text: Step For the stairs state f[i] = number of ways to reach step i transition the last move was 1 step (from i − 1) or 2 steps (from i − 2): f[i] = f[i−1] + f[i−2]
order i increasing

The values grow like Fibonacci numbers: f[5000] has over 1000 digits, so the table holds big numbers from 第8章(P1255). Only the last two entries are needed, so two variables replace the whole table. A bee walking from cell m to cell n is the same recurrence with n − m steps (P2437).

A pawn moves only right or down. The number of ways to reach a cell = ways to the cell above + ways to the cell on the left; blocked cells (x) have 0 ways. Fill row by row, so both neighbours are ready.
Here 9 = 5 (above) + 4 (left). The first row and first column have exactly 1 way each until a blocked cell cuts them off.
Shifting every coordinate by 1 gives the table a row 0 and column 0 of zeros, so the edges need no special case. The counts reach about 1017 for a 20 × 20 board: use long long (P1002).

Some transitions add up many earlier entries. Stack output orders split by "where does the first element leave": f[i] = Σ f[k] · f[i−1−k], the Catalan numbers (P1044). "Prepend a number at most half of the current one" sums f[1 … i/2] (P1028).
Count the ways to spend exactly m on distinct dishes. Add dishes one at a time; with dish a, every amount j gains the ways that reached j − a before (P1164).
Loop j downwards. Going upwards would let the same dish be used again within one round.
Tiling a 2 × n wall with dominoes and L-shapes: list how the right end can look, and write one transition per shape (P1990).
Solve the same problem on smaller input: Hanoi, memoisation, nested text, divide and conquer.

Recursion (递归) writes the answer for a problem in terms of the same problem on smaller input, top- down. It suits problems whose structure is nested: expressions inside brackets, a board split into quarters, a string built from copies of itself.

To move n disks, trust the function to move n − 1: clear them to the spare peg, move the largest, then bring the n − 1 back. The base case n = 0 does nothing. The count is 2n − 1.

Write the recursive call as if it already works for smaller n; then only one level has to be right. Moving black and white pieces into alternate order (P1259) has the same "solve n from n − 1" structure.

The plain recursion calls itself several times per level and explodes. Only 20 × 20 × 20 different arguments can occur, so store each result the first time (P1464). Check the guard order exactly as the statement gives it: the "≤ 0" rule comes before the "> 20" rule.

A bracket inside the text is the same problem again: the decoder calls itself when it meets "[" and returns at the matching "]" (P1928). An exponent written in powers of 2 is again "write a number in powers of 2" (P1010).

title: Divide and conquer: halves and quarters

text: COW 8
C

Each doubling appends a copy rotated by one place. A position in the second half maps back to one position in the first half, so halve until the position lies inside the original string: O(log n) steps even for n = 1018 (P3612).

Board and picture problems split the same way: a 2k board with one missing cell is covered by placing one L-shape in the centre and solving four quarters (P1228); the totem picture is three copies of the smaller picture (P1498).
The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. Recurrence: write the state, transition, base cases and order before coding.
2. Stairs: f[i] = f[i−1] + f[i−2]; counts grow fast → long long or big numbers.
3. Grid paths: f[i][j] = f[i−1][j] + f[i][j−1]; blocked cells are 0; pad row 0 and column 0.
4. Catalan: f[i] = Σ f[k] · f[i−1−k] (stack orders, brackets, trees).
5. Exact-sum counting with each item once: loop the amount downwards.
6. Recursion: trust the call for smaller input; get one level and the base case right.
7. Hanoi: n−1 aside, move the largest, n−1 back; 2ⁿ − 1 moves.
8. Repeated arguments → memoise; keep the statement's guard order.
9. Nested text → a recursive parser that returns at the closing bracket.
10. Huge positions in self-similar strings → map back through halvings in O(log n).
